column2: A systematic review on cybersecurity of robotic systems: vulnerabilities trends, threats, attacks, challenges, and proposed framework
column7: The review states that ROS lacks a mechanism for regulating information distribution between nodes, allowing a network-visible node to transmit information on a topic. It also summarizes false-data injection, unauthorized node publishing, and unauthorized publisher/subscriber attacks.
column11: Primary code. Explicitly discussed and supported by external studies, but not independently evaluated by this paper.

column2: A systematic review on cybersecurity of robotic systems: vulnerabilities trends, threats, attacks, challenges, and proposed framework
column7: The paper explicitly states that ROS messages can be transmitted without encryption, enabling eavesdropping, and discusses TLS/DTLS and encryption-based secure channels as countermeasures.
column11: Plaintext communication is explicitly described, but the authors perform no packet capture or independent ROS experiment.

column2: A systematic review on cybersecurity of robotic systems: vulnerabilities trends, threats, attacks, challenges, and proposed framework
column7: The review identifies poor authentication and unauthorized ROS nodes as common weaknesses and summarizes an authentication-server architecture intended to control which nodes may publish or subscribe.
column11: Authentication weakness is explicit, but evidence is a secondary synthesis of earlier work.

column2: A systematic review on cybersecurity of robotic systems: vulnerabilities trends, threats, attacks, challenges, and proposed framework
column7: The paper reviews ROS middleware DoS attacks caused by large numbers of unauthorized publishers or subscribers. It reports increased processing, storage consumption, network unresponsiveness, message delay, and packet loss.
column8: Sec. 3.1.1, p. 13; Sec. 4 discussion, p. 27; Table 11, pp. 29–30
column11: The DoS mechanism is consistent with malicious high-rate publishing and connection occupation, but the experiments belong to cited studies rather than this review.

column2: Cyber security of robots: A comprehensive survey
column7: The survey reports that an attacker inside a ROS network can send shutdown commands, publish adulterated messages, manipulate velocity commands, inject false or malicious data, and access ROS services without sufficient authorization.
column11: Primary code. The weakness and attack consequences are explicitly synthesized from previous studies, but this paper does not independently execute or evaluate the attacks.

column2: Cyber security of robots: A comprehensive survey
column7: The paper identifies unsecured ROS-to-ROS and node-to-node ports that communicate in plaintext. It also summarizes plain-text communications, unencrypted storage, and encryption-based countermeasures for protecting ROS node communication.
column11: Directly matches absent channel protection in ROS 1, but the evidence is secondary and no packet-level experiment is performed by the survey authors.

column2: Cyber security of robots: A comprehensive survey
column7: The survey explicitly describes weak ROS authentication, unauthorized or rogue nodes, and the ability of malicious nodes to execute commands or alter robot behavior. It reviews authentication nodes, authorization servers, web tokens, and trusted-node mechanisms as countermeasures.
column11: The paper distinguishes unauthorized nodes and weak authentication from authorization of topic/service operations, supporting a separate LNA code.

column2: Cyber security of robots: A comprehensive survey
column7: The paper states that publicly exposed ROS instances allow malicious users to access sensors and read images or other sensor information. It also cites an Internet-wide scan reporting more than 100 ROS Master instances accessible from the public Internet.
column11: Explicit evidence of external network reachability and public ROS Master exposure. The Internet scan was conducted by a cited study rather than by the survey authors.

column2: Robotics Cyber Security: Vulnerabilities, Attacks, Countermeasures, and Recommendations
column7: The paper reviews cryptographic protection for ROS communication channels and the integration of TLS and DTLS into the ROS core. This explicitly indicates that baseline ROS communication requires additional channel protection to preserve confidentiality.
column8: Sec. V-E, “Cryptographic Solutions & Protocols,” p. 21
column11: Primary code. The evidence is a secondary synthesis of cited ROS security studies; the authors do not independently intercept ROS traffic or evaluate plaintext communication.

column2: Robotics Cyber Security: Vulnerabilities, Attacks, Countermeasures, and Recommendations
column7: The reviewed ROS security solution introduces fine-grained control over permission to publish, subscribe, or consume data. The paper therefore explicitly recognizes the need to restrict ROS communication operations through authorization controls.
column8: Sec. V-E, “Cryptographic Solutions & Protocols,” p. 21
column11: This is discussed through a cited countermeasure rather than an independently demonstrated unauthorized publication, subscription, or service call.

column2: Security in Robot Operating Systems (ROS): Analytical Review Study
column7: The paper states that ROS publishers cannot control who consumes their information and that unauthorized nodes can record data or publish injected messages. It further identifies access control over topic publishing and subscription as a necessary protection mechanism.
column8: Introduction, p. 2; Table 4, pp. 8–9; Table 6, p. 11
column11: Primary code. The issue is explicitly analyzed as a ROS security weakness, but evidence is synthesized from prior studies rather than independently demonstrated.

column2: Security in Robot Operating Systems (ROS): Analytical Review Study
column7: ROS 1 network traffic is described as being transmitted in a basic, unprotected form, making it susceptible to packet eavesdropping, man-in-the-middle attacks, and network hijacking. The review states that encryption is required to protect confidential ROS information.
column8: Sec. IV, p. 7; Table 4, p. 8
column11: Directly supports absent channel protection in ROS 1, but the authors conduct no packet capture or communication experiment.

column2: Security in Robot Operating Systems (ROS): Analytical Review Study
column7: The ROS 1 API is described as essentially anonymous, with no mechanism ensuring that received information originated from a legitimate node. The paper recommends cryptographic source verification and authentication.
column8: Sec. IV, p. 7; Table 4, pp. 8–9
column11: Supports missing node identity verification. The paper does not independently implement node impersonation or authentication bypass.

column2: Security in Robot Operating Systems (ROS): Analytical Review Study
column7: The comparative analysis reviews Internet exposure detection through scans of ROS Master nodes. The open directions recommend testing reachability from outside the organization and installing firewalls to prevent exposure to public networks.
column8: Table 6, p. 11; Sec. VII and Table 7, p. 12
column11: External reachability is explicitly treated as a ROS security problem, but the scan results originate from a cited study.

column2: Security in Robot Operating Systems (ROS): Analytical Review Study
column7: The review identifies a ROS denial-of-service scenario caused by unauthorized publishing at a high frequency, corresponding to malicious traffic overwhelming ROS communication or processing resources.
column8: Table 6, p. 11
column11: Explicit high-rate publishing evidence supports flow-control and QoS weakness, but no attack is executed by the review authors.

column2: Who Controls Your Robot? An Evaluation of ROS Security Mechanisms
column7: The authors determine that SROS 2/DDS-Security encrypts transmitted application data but sends access-control policies, node names, and topic names in plaintext. Consequently, it does not provide metadata confidentiality.
column8: Sec. VII-J and Table I, PDF pp. 5–6, paper pp. 64–65
column11: Primary code. The finding was evaluated using ROS 2 Eloquent and directly matches leakage of policy and identity metadata despite security being enabled.

column2: Who Controls Your Robot? An Evaluation of ROS Security Mechanisms
column7: The study concludes that unprotected ROS 1 provides no confidentiality for network communication. A MITM attacker can read ROS traffic, while encryption mechanisms such as SROS, Secure ROS, TLS/DTLS, AES, and VPN are required to protect it.
column8: Secs. V-A, VI-A and VII-A; Table I, PDF pp. 2–5
column11: ROS 1 confidentiality is a direct evaluation criterion rather than an incidental background statement.

column2: Who Controls Your Robot? An Evaluation of ROS Security Mechanisms
column7: The attacker model allows an adversary to establish rogue ROS nodes, modify or inject traffic, and impersonate a compromised node. The evaluation finds that default ROS 1 lacks integrity and sender-authentication protection.
column8: Secs. V-A–V-B, VI-C and VII-A; Table I, PDF pp. 2–5
column11: The paper analytically evaluates sender identity and communication authenticity, although it does not execute a separate node-registration hijacking experiment.

column2: Who Controls Your Robot? An Evaluation of ROS Security Mechanisms
column7: Default ROS 1 is evaluated as providing no access control. The paper explains that a compromised or rogue node must be restricted to only the topics it legitimately needs to publish or subscribe to, and compares mechanisms offering node-, host-, IP-, or certificate-based access control.
column8: Sec. VI-D, Sec. VII-A–VII-H and Table I, PDF pp. 3–6
column11: Direct evaluation of unrestricted topic access and the ability of protection mechanisms to constrain publishers and subscribers.

column2: Who Controls Your Robot? An Evaluation of ROS Security Mechanisms
column7: Because DDS security extensions are disabled in the default ROS 2 configuration, ROS 2 provides no communication-integrity or source-authentication guarantee. A receiving node therefore cannot cryptographically verify that a message originated from a legitimate publisher.
column8: Sec. I-B, Sec. VI-C and Sec. VII-I; PDF pp. 1, 3 and 6
column11: The paper directly evaluates the missing authenticity property. No concrete forged /tf or shared-topic publisher attack is executed, but the missing publisher binding is explicitly established for default ROS 2.

column2: Robot Operating System 2: The Need for a Holistic Security Approach to Robotic Architectures
column7: DDS-Security allows discovery, liveliness, RTPS messages, metadata, and serialized payloads to receive different protection levels: NONE, SIGN, or ENCRYPT. When discovery or metadata is only signed, participant identifiers, GUIDs, endpoint information, topology information, sequence numbers, locators, and other metadata remain visible in plaintext. The paper explains that clear-text GUID and discovery information may support masquerading and topology reconstruction.
column8: Governance policy discussion, pp. 4 and 6; “Performance versus security models,” pp. 9–12; especially pp. 9–10
column11: Primary code. The authors configure multiple DDS-Security protection combinations and measure their behavior and performance. The confidentiality gap is configuration-dependent rather than a claim that full encryption is impossible.

column2: Robot Operating System 2: The Need for a Holistic Security Approach to Robotic Architectures
column7: ROS 2 DDS-Security depends on locally stored identity certificates, private keys, governance policies, and participant permission policies. The authors identify unresolved responsibility for policy creation and signing, note that security plug-ins are not necessarily digitally signed or vetted, and emphasize that credentials and policy files require stronger lifecycle and trust management.
column8: DDS security policy and plug-in discussion, pp. 4–7
column11: The standard supports CA signatures for governance and permission policies, so the paper does not establish that every deployment leaves them unprotected. The code reflects residual credential and policy-management exposure rather than complete absence of protection.

column2: Robot Operating System 2: The Need for a Holistic Security Approach to Robotic Architectures
column7: DDS-Security protects data in motion but does not isolate local operating-system processes, memory, hardware components, or cryptographic libraries. The paper describes a malicious local spy process that may observe leakages from other processes and recover sensitive information such as encryption keys.
column8: “Systematic security review,” pp. 6–8; “Software,” p. 8; “Recommendations,” p. 13
column11: This is an explicit architectural gap outside the DDS messaging layer, but no spy process, cross-process memory attack, or key-recovery experiment is implemented.

column2: Robot Operating System 2: The Need for a Holistic Security Approach to Robotic Architectures
column7: The authors warn that hardware and software obtained from untrusted suppliers may introduce backdoors. They also state that DDS security service providers and plug-ins are not required to follow a signed-provider model comparable to mature cryptographic architectures, allowing a malicious component or spy process to enter the software ecosystem.
column8: Security plug-in discussion, p. 7; “Recommendations,” p. 13
column11: The supply-chain risk is directly identified, but the paper does not replace a DDS plug-in, compromise OpenSSL, or demonstrate a malicious dependency in the evaluated ROS 2 system.

column2: Understanding Misconfigurations in ROS: An Empirical Study and Current Approaches
column7: The empirical taxonomy directly identifies interaction and configuration faults involving topic and resource-name mismatches, incompatible message formats, absent or conflicting publishers, missing or incorrect nodes, namespaces, remappings, launch-file composition, environment variables, parameter-name dead writes, and missing or duplicate transforms. Figure 4 demonstrates a mistyped topic name that leaves the subscriber disconnected from the intended publisher.
column8: Sec. 3.3, pp. 5–7; Figs. 3–4; Listing 1
column11: Primary code. These faults originate in relationships and configuration bindings among ROS entities. Incorrect behavior, missing data, or node startup failure are consequences rather than separate defect codes.

column2: Understanding Misconfigurations in ROS: An Empirical Study and Current Approaches
column7: The study directly identifies semantic faults involving physical units, message-content constraints, color formats, image and point-cloud transformations, incorrect TF values or conventions, URDF properties, calibration, control parameters, robot-localization assumptions, and application/environment-dependent configuration. These cases may use syntactically valid and correctly connected interfaces while carrying an incorrect physical or behavioral meaning.
column8: Sec. 3.3, pp. 6–8; Fig. 3
column11: Use BSE for incorrect values or meanings, such as degrees versus radians, invalid TF geometry, incorrect wheel radius, unsuitable PID gains, or an inappropriate planner. Missing topic or parameter bindings remain ICF.

column2: Understanding Misconfigurations in ROS: An Empirical Study and Current Approaches
column7: The taxonomy explicitly analyzes queue-size errors, frequency mismatches, stale data, message synchronization failures, and launch-time race conditions. In the stereo-vision example, slow disparity processing causes faster image streams to fill queues and overwrite messages before synchronized inputs are available.
column8: Sec. 3.3, pp. 5–7; Fig. 5
column11: Queue overflow, missed timing assumptions, stale messages, and synchronization failures originate in runtime execution and timing mechanisms. They should not be recoded as ICF merely because communication is ultimately affected.

column2: The Role of Security in Human-Robot Shared Environments: A Case Study in ROS-based Surveillance Robots
column7: ROS uses anonymous publish/subscribe semantics, weak authorization, no access-level definitions, and no conflict-resolution mechanism. A network participant can subscribe to arbitrary topics, kill nodes, send direct robot commands, or concurrently publish velocity commands that override legitimate control.
column8: Sec. III, p. 3; Conclusion, p. 6
column11: Primary code. The paper explicitly analyzes unrestricted publication, subscription, node control, and command injection as central ROS security flaws. No original attack execution is reported.

column2: The Role of Security in Human-Robot Shared Environments: A Case Study in ROS-based Surveillance Robots
column7: Communication between ROS nodes is transmitted in clear text over TCP/IP or UDP/IP. The MD5 check verifies only message-structure compatibility and does not encrypt content, allowing an unauthorized listener to intercept messages, interpret their contents, and construct spoofed messages.
column8: Sec. III, p. 3
column11: Direct evidence of absent channel encryption in ROS 1. The STOP architecture consequently proposes TLS/SSL, application-layer message encryption, VPNs, and encrypted storage.

column2: The Role of Security in Human-Robot Shared Environments: A Case Study in ROS-based Surveillance Robots
column7: ROS exposes unprotected TCP ports without authentication, nodes do not know the identities of communicating peers, and the system provides no sender verification or message-authenticity checking. Malicious talkers and replacement publishers/listeners can therefore join the system.
column8: Sec. III, p. 3
column11: Distinct from topic authorization: this code concerns the inability to establish and verify the identity of ROS nodes and message senders.

column2: The Role of Security in Human-Robot Shared Environments: A Case Study in ROS-based Surveillance Robots
column7: The paper states that ROS provides no QoS mechanisms, leaves communication management to individual nodes, does not compact similar messages, and makes no effort to reduce communication volume. High communication volume hampers time-critical applications and enables network clogging and DoS conditions.
column8: Sec. III, p. 3
column11: Explicitly concerns missing QoS, traffic control, communication-volume management, and resistance to excessive requests or publishing.

column2: The Role of Security in Human-Robot Shared Environments: A Case Study in ROS-based Surveillance Robots
column7: The centralized ROS Master naming service is described as a scalability bottleneck that is not designed to process a large volume of requests and may be exposed to DoS. In the STOP project, the authors reject a shared Master as impractical and instead assign a separate ROS Master to each robot.
column8: Sec. III, p. 3; Sec. IV-A and IV-C, pp. 4–5
column11: The centralized dependency and bottleneck are explicit, but the paper does not crash the Master or demonstrate complete graph-discovery failure. Partial is therefore more defensible than Full.

column2: A Study on ROS Vulnerabilities and Countermeasure
column7: ROS does not authenticate communication between the Master and nodes. By setting the attacker’s ROS_MASTER_URI and ROS_HOSTNAME, the attacker connects to the victim environment without further authentication and controls TurtleSim remotely.
column11: Primary code. The authors explicitly identify missing authentication to the Master as the common enabling cause of most demonstrated attacks.

column2: A Study on ROS Vulnerabilities and Countermeasure
column7: After entering the ROS network, the attacker can access and publish control topics. The attacker records all KOBUKI messages using rosbag record -a, replays them to reproduce robot movement, and registers a service with an existing name to replace the legitimate service.
column11: Covers unauthorized topic access, command replay, service registration, and service replacement. Rosbag is an attack utility here, not the underlying defect.

column2: A Study on ROS Vulnerabilities and Countermeasure
column7: ROS XML-RPC communication is transmitted without encryption. An intermediary attacker can observe the communication history and manipulate exchanged data to control the robot remotely.
column11: The proposed Diffie–Hellman and AES-256 countermeasure confirms that absent communication encryption is the identified root problem.

column2: ROSploit: Cybersecurity Tool for ROS
column7: The Master-scan component invokes getSystemState() and obtains the complete list of active nodes, topics, and services. The exploitation component can then insert itself between two nodes on a selected topic and modify their communication.
column8: “Threat Model” and “ROSploit,” PDF pp. 1–2; Fig. 1, p. 2
column11: Primary code. The implemented tool directly demonstrates unrestricted discovery of ROS resources and the ability to access and manipulate topic communication without an application-defined authorization policy.

column2: ROSploit: Cybersecurity Tool for ROS
column7: ROSploit sends ordinary XML-RPC and TCPROS requests to open ports and can interact with identified ROS nodes without presenting a node certificate or other identity credential. The paper also identifies unauthorized publishers and subscribers as central ROS threats.
column8: “Security for ROS,” p. 1; “Threat Model,” p. 1; “ROSploit,” p. 2
column11: The tool behavior is consistent with absent peer authentication, but the paper does not separately implement or measure a node-authentication bypass experiment.

column2: ROSploit: Cybersecurity Tool for ROS
column7: The tool supports a MITM mode that inserts itself into communication between two ROS nodes and allows the user to inspect or alter exchanged data. The paper contrasts baseline ROS with SROS, which adds TLS encryption to address existing communication vulnerabilities.
column8: “Security for ROS,” p. 1; “ROSploit,” p. 2
column11: The communication channel is treated as insufficiently protected, but the paper does not report packet-capture results or independently quantify plaintext-data exposure.

column2: Scanning the Internet for ROS: A View of Security in Robotics Research
column7: The authors scanned approximately 3.7 billion public IPv4 addresses for the default ROS Master port and repeatedly identified more than 100 publicly reachable ROS Masters. Publicly exposed systems revealed nodes, topics, services, parameters, sensors, actuators, robot types and research activity patterns.
column8: Abstract and Sec. I, p. 1; Sec. IV, pp. 2–3; Sec. V and Tables I–III, pp. 3–6
column11: Primary code. External network exposure is the central measured defect. The study directly establishes that ROS Masters and Rosbridge instances were reachable beyond their intended trust boundaries.

column2: Scanning the Internet for ROS: A View of Security in Robotics Research
column7: A remote host could query ROS graph information, subscribe to camera and point-cloud topics, publish messages to change Baxter’s face and joint angles, invoke speech and neck-control services, and thereby control robot sensors and actuators without a ROS-level authorization decision.
column8: Sec. VI-B–VI-C, pp. 6–7; Fig. 2, p. 7
column11: The proof-of-concept was conducted with explicit operator consent. It demonstrates unauthorized topic access, publication and service invocation that would otherwise be available to any similarly connected attacker.

column2: Scanning the Internet for ROS: A View of Security in Robotics Research
column7: The paper states that the ROS Master trusts every node that connects to it. For the Herb2 penetration test, the researchers only needed to set ROS_MASTER_URI, ROS_IP and local hostname resolution before their remote ROS node could interact with the target system; no ROS node credential or identity certificate was required.
column8: Sec. I, p. 1; Sec. III, p. 2; Sec. VI-C, p. 7
column11: Distinct from authorization: the remote node was accepted as a ROS participant without proving that it was a legitimate node belonging to the robot deployment.

column2: Scanning the Internet for ROS: A View of Security in Robotics Research
column7: During the authors’ penetration test of their publicly exposed Baxter robot, remote XML-RPC access allowed them to inspect and modify rosparam values. They explain that changing arm-controller PID gains could place the robot in a dangerous state and cause unexpected oscillation.
column8: Sec. IV, p. 3; Sec. VI-B, pp. 6–7
column11: Direct experimental evidence of remotely modifying Parameter Server values without a ROS-level authorization check. The dangerous PID effect is a security impact and is not separately coded as a reliability fault.

column2: Security on ROS: Analyzing and Exploiting Vulnerabilities of ROS-Based Systems
column7: The paper states that ROS provides no authentication mechanism for managing communication between nodes. Consequently, ROS peers cannot cryptographically establish that the entity sending or forwarding communication is a legitimate robot component.
column8: Introduction, p. 1; Sec. III-B, p. 2
column11: The weakness is explicitly identified, but the implemented experiment impersonates endpoints through ARP poisoning rather than registering a rogue ROS node or demonstrating a ROS-level authentication bypass.

column2: Security on ROS: Analyzing and Exploiting Vulnerabilities of ROS-Based Systems
column7: The authors state that ROS lacks authorization controls and allows any computer on the network to listen to desired topics. Their tool targets the /speech_to_text topic and can be adapted to alter messages of any known ROS message type on any intercepted topic.
column8: Introduction, p. 1; Sec. IV, pp. 3–4
column11: Topic communication is experimentally accessed and modified without an application authorization decision. Coverage is Partial because the attack captures network traffic rather than subscribing or publishing through the ROS Master API.

column2: Security Controller Synthesis for ROS-based Robot
column7: The paper states that a ROS node may publish data to arbitrary topics without prior authorization. An attacker on the same network can therefore send false speed, position, or navigation information, causing the robot to execute unexpected actions or enter dangerous regions. The proposed security controller limits speed, stops near people, and returns the robot from the staircase to a safe location.
column8: Sec. IV-A, pp. 3–4; Figs. 2–4
column11: Primary code. The weakness and mitigation logic are explicit, but the paper does not implement and measure an actual malicious publisher or topic-injection attack.

column2: Security Controller Synthesis for ROS-based Robot
column7: The false-information scenario is enabled because publishers can interact with ROS topics without pre-authentication. The system therefore cannot establish that a node sending commands is an authorized participant before accepting its messages.
column8: Sec. IV-A, p. 3
column11: Separate from authorization: this code captures the absence of participant identity verification. No authentication-bypass experiment or rogue-node registration trace is reported.

column2: Security Controller Synthesis for ROS-based Robot
column7: The authors explain that every node can publish arbitrary content to topics subscribed to by a target node, enabling traffic-flooding DoS. Their controller monitors message count, CPU usage, CPU temperature, RAM usage, and battery consumption, shuts down the affected robot, and assigns its task to a standby robot.
column8: Sec. IV-B, pp. 4–6; Figs. 5–7
column11: The Gazebo scenario demonstrates the security-controller response to a detected DoS condition. However, the paper does not specify an implemented flooding node, publication rate, packet volume, threshold values, or measured resource-exhaustion curve, so Partial is more defensible than Full.

column2: Penetration Testing ROS
column7: Anonymous attackers can query the complete ROS graph and invoke unrestricted Master and Slave API operations. ROSPenTo uses forged publisherUpdate calls to disconnect legitimate publishers, attach unauthorized publishers, isolate services and inject false sensor data. Roschaos can unregister publishers, subscribers, services and complete nodes, or remotely invoke node shutdown.
column11: Primary code. The tools directly demonstrate unauthorized topic manipulation, false publication, service disruption, action interference and node termination.

column2: Penetration Testing ROS
column7: ROS 1 does not authenticate XML-RPC callers. Node identity is derived entirely from attacker-controlled parameters such as caller_id, node name and API URI, without cryptographic proof. This permits attackers to impersonate the Master, publishers, nodes or service providers when invoking registration, update and shutdown methods.
column11: The lack of identity validation is not merely background: ROSPenTo and Roschaos rely on forged caller identities to make unauthorized API calls appear legitimate.

column2: Penetration Testing ROS
column7: The ROS Parameter Server applies no ownership or namespace-based access restriction and gives anonymous clients read and write access. ROSPenTo demonstrates unsubscribing a C++ node from legitimate parameter updates and sending a forged paramUpdate, changing the value observed locally while the value stored on the Parameter Server remains unchanged. Roschaos can also delete or manipulate parameters and subscriptions.
column11: Direct experimental evidence of unauthorized parameter inspection, update, deletion and desynchronization. The attack can cause different nodes to observe inconsistent values for the same parameter.

column2: Penetration Testing ROS
column7: The paper states that ROS 1 TCP/UDP communication has no confidentiality protection or authenticated encryption, making network eavesdropping straightforward. It contrasts baseline ROS with SROS and other secure ROS variants that add encryption.
column11: The confidentiality weakness is explicit, but ROSPenTo and Roschaos mainly exploit XML-RPC authorization flaws rather than presenting an independent packet-capture or plaintext-content experiment.

column2: Novel Denial-of-Service Attacks Against Cloud-Based Multi-Robot Systems
column7: A malicious ROS publisher can increase its publication rate from 4 Hz to 400 Hz and continuously send dummy messages with valid content. ROS provides no effective mechanism in the evaluated configuration to constrain the publisher rate or prevent the messages from filling the wireless router queue and consuming subscriber computation resources. The attack substantially increases latency, packet loss and critical-node processing time.
column11: Primary code. The paper directly implements and quantitatively evaluates high-rate publishing, communication congestion and resource exhaustion in ROS Melodic.

column2: Data Tampering Attack Design for ROS-Based Object Detection and Tracking Robotic Platform
column7: TCPROS and XMLRPC lack authentication or identity verification. The authors exploit this weakness through ARP spoofing and by introducing a malicious publisher, forcing a legitimate subscriber to communicate with the attacker-controlled node.
column8: Abstract; Sec. IV-B, pp. 4–5; Conclusion, p. 6
column11: Primary code. Authentication weakness is directly analyzed and experimentally exploited on the physical ROS platform.

column2: Data Tampering Attack Design for ROS-Based Object Detection and Tracking Robotic Platform
column7: ROS node messages are transmitted in cleartext. The authors intercept the 48-byte serialized /cmd_vel control message using a MITM attack, identify the linear and angular velocity fields with Wireshark, modify the values and forward the altered message to the robot.
column8: Sec. IV-B(a), p. 4; Figs. 5–8, pp. 4–5
column11: Cleartext TCPROS traffic is directly captured and modified; this is stronger than a general capability claim.

column2: Data Tampering Attack Design for ROS-Based Object Detection and Tracking Robotic Platform
column7: The attack tool invokes getSystemState and publisherUpdate, creates a malicious node with the required message type and injects fake images into the object-detection node without authorization. The injected data prevents correct target detection and disrupts robot tracking.
column8: Sec. IV-B(b), p. 5; Figs. 9–12, p. 5
column11: Direct experimental evidence of unauthorized publishing and false-data injection through ROS APIs.

column2: Analysis of Attacks on Robotic Operation System
column7: The ROS Master API accepts publisher, subscriber and service registration or deregistration without authentication. Using roschaos, the authors unregister the /publisher node, after which the listener stops receiving messages even though the publisher process remains active. The ROS Slave API publisherUpdate method is also unauthenticated; ROSPenTo sends a forged empty publisher list directly to /listener, causing it to disconnect from the legitimate publisher.
column11: Primary code. Both demonstrated attacks share the same primary root cause: unauthenticated ROS control-plane API calls.

column2: Analysis of Attacks on Robotic Operation System
column7: The paper states that ROS TCP/UDP communication is not encrypted and that eavesdropping is easy, allowing any network participant to read application data.
column8: Introduction and Sec. 1, pp. 41–42; PDF pp. 1–2
column11: Explicit ROS 1 plaintext weakness, but the authors do not perform packet interception or independently evaluate confidentiality loss.

column2: Cyberattacks on Self-Driving Cars and Surgical and Eldercare Robots
column7: The paper states that any ROS node can publish data without proper authorization, inject malicious instructions and subscribe to arbitrary topics to obtain sensitive information. It further notes that application-level protection cannot prevent malicious publishers from sending messages or unauthorized subscribers from subscribing to topics.
column8: Sec. 2.1, p. 2; Sec. 2.2, p. 3; Table 1, p. 4
column11: Primary code. The vulnerability is directly reviewed, but the paper does not independently implement or evaluate an unauthorized publishing/subscription attack.

column2: Cyberattacks on Self-Driving Cars and Surgical and Eldercare Robots
column7: The paper describes weak authentication in ROS and states that the ROS Master can register a new malicious node without detecting the attacker. Authentication servers and validation of nodes are reviewed as necessary countermeasures.
column11: The evidence concerns malicious-node registration and node validation, distinct from authorization to publish or subscribe.

column2: Cyberattacks on Self-Driving Cars and Surgical and Eldercare Robots
column7: The paper explicitly states that ROS messages may be transmitted without encryption, enabling eavesdropping. It reviews SSL/TLS, symmetric encryption and DDS cryptographic plug-ins as mechanisms for protecting ROS communication.
column8: Sec. 2.2, p. 3; Table 1, p. 4; Sec. 3.1, p. 7
column11: Plaintext ROS communication is explicit, but no packet capture or independent confidentiality experiment is reported.

column2: Cyberattacks on Self-Driving Cars and Surgical and Eldercare Robots
column7: The review explains that an attacker can publish a large volume of bogus ROS messages, bombard subscribers, impose heavy processing load and prevent meaningful processing. It also notes that application-level encryption does not prevent a malicious publisher from launching a high-frequency DoS attack.
column11: Directly matches malicious high-rate publishing and absent traffic regulation, but the attack is summarized from earlier work.

column2: ROS Network Security for a Swing Doors Automation in a Robotized Hospital
column7: The paper explicitly identifies unencrypted TCPROS message transmission and unencrypted data storage as major ROS 1 security problems. It explains that attackers may capture confidential medical information or perform MITM packet modification, and the proposed architecture therefore relies on network isolation and optional encryption for confidential nodes.
column8: Abstract; Sec. I, p. 1; Sec. II, pp. 1–2; Sec. IV-B, p. 3; Conclusion, p. 4
column11: Primary code. Plaintext ROS 1 communication is a direct object of the study and a primary driver of the proposed architecture, although the authors do not perform packet interception themselves.

column2: ROS Network Security for a Swing Doors Automation in a Robotized Hospital
column7: The paper reviews authentication-server, certificate, HMAC and authorization/authentication-node solutions and states that external devices must pass authentication and authorization before entering the proposed hospital network. Connections between ROS nodes may also require additional authentication.
column8: Sec. III, p. 2; Sec. IV-B, p. 3; Conclusion, p. 4
column11: Missing authentication is explicitly treated as a security requirement, but the paper does not demonstrate node impersonation, malicious registration or authentication bypass.

column2: An Analysis of DoS Attack on Robot Operating System
column7: The authors create large numbers of malicious publisher and subscriber nodes to overload ROS communication. Subscriber attacks force a publisher to answer excessive data requests, while publisher attacks flood a subscriber with messages and consume processing, storage and network resources. The experiments demonstrate substantial delay and packet loss that increase with attack volume.
column11: Primary code. This directly matches malicious high-rate publishing/subscribing and inadequate flow or resource control in ROS 1.

column2: An Analysis of DoS Attack on Robot Operating System

The security analysis concludes that a compromised node can access only memory associated with its own protection key, rather than other nodes or the client library.
column8: Sec. V-A–F, pp. 10553–10556; Figs. 10–17; Table II
column11: A second evidence row is justified because it records the direct evaluation of the same defect family. ROSEC incurs 6.4% overhead in the camera-based real-world application.

column2: Support Remote Attestation for Decentralized Robot Operating System (ROS) Using Trusted Execution Environment
column7: The paper states that DDS Security provides authentication, access control and cryptographic protection while assuming the local machine is trusted. A compromised ROS 2 node or privileged local attacker may exploit masquerading credentials, alter registered services, access private keys or modify security configuration. The proposed architecture places DDS, encrypted files, parameters, policies and secrets inside SCONE/SGX and uses an attested ID and Permission Manager to verify nodes and control policy updates.
column8: Abstract and Sec. I, p. 693; Sec. II, p. 694; Fig. 1
column11: Directly matches inadequate local protection of credentials and policies. Coverage is Partial because the architecture is not implemented or experimentally evaluated. Sensitive-data theft also implies IMP-DS, but integrity protection is the principal emphasis.

column2: Quantifying DDS-Cerberus Network Control Overhead
column7: The paper identifies node impersonation as a principal DDS security weakness: an attacker may create a rogue publisher or subscriber, pose as a trusted node and obtain unauthorized permission to send or read data. DDS-C integrates Kerberos authentication into ROS 2/DDS so that every publisher and subscriber must obtain a valid ticket using its assigned keytab before participating in communication. An impersonated node without the correct keytab is denied a ticket and cannot publish or subscribe. The implemented ROS 2 testbed measures the additional authentication traffic generated by this mechanism.
column11: Primary code. Authentication is implemented and exercised in the testbed, but the experiments do not actually launch a rogue or impersonated node. The mechanism authenticates participants before communication rather than cryptographically signing every individual ROS 2 message.

column2: Decentralized Information-Flow Control for ROS2
column7: The paper explains that SROS2 restricts which topics an application may publish or subscribe to, but once an authorized application receives protected data, ROS 2 provides no mechanism for the original data owner to control how that application subsequently republishes or derives information from the data. A legitimate subscriber can therefore relay protected content to another, less protected topic and cause data exfiltration. Picaros binds DIFC labels to individual data objects using attribute-based encryption and enforces no-reads-up and no-writes-down rules across downstream application chains.
column8: Abstract and Sec. I, pp. 1–2; Sec. II, pp. 3–5; Figs. 1–2; Sec. III–IV, pp. 6–11
column11: Primary code. The study defines and implements message/data-object-level confidentiality properties and evaluates the enforcing prototype. The cases are author-constructed application pipelines rather than independently observed real-world leaks.

column2: ROSRV: Runtime Verification for Robots
column7: The paper identifies application-level behavioral safety violations that are not prevented by ordinary ROS, including the LandShark firing while its gun points toward itself, leaving a defined safe zone and tipping over because of unsafe speed or acceleration. ROSRV generates monitors from formal event specifications and can drop trigger messages or modify motion messages when the corresponding behavioral property is violated. The safe-trigger, safe-zone and logging monitors are demonstrated on the LandShark platform.
column8: Sec. 2.1, p. 3; Sec. 3.1, pp. 4–5; Appendix A, p. 8; Figs. 2 and 4
column11: Primary code. The monitored conditions are explicit behavioral and domain-safety properties. They are not implementation, wiring or scheduling faults.

column2: ROSRV: Runtime Verification for Robots
column7: The paper states that any ROS node may publish or subscribe to arbitrary topics and may issue sensitive commands such as shutting down another node. RVMaster checks the requesting host, topic and command against user-defined [Publishers], [Subscribers] and [Commands] policies. In the attacker-node demonstration, unauthorized nodes are prevented from publishing to protected topics and killing legal nodes.
column8: Sec. 1, pp. 1–2; Sec. 2.1, p. 3; Sec. 3.2, pp. 5–6; Appendix A, p. 8; Fig. 5
column11: Directly evaluated unrestricted topic and command access. The policy covers both publish/subscribe permissions and privileged ROS Master operations.

column2: ROSRV: Runtime Verification for Robots
column7: ROS node names are self-reported, and a newly created node with an existing name may replace the legitimate node. The paper describes an attacker killing a navigation node and creating a fake node that publishes bogus messages. ROSRV’s [Nodes] policy binds permitted node names to designated host identities, and the demonstration shows that an attacker cannot pretend to be an existing legal node.
column8: Sec. 1, pp. 1–2; Sec. 2.1, p. 3; Sec. 3.2, pp. 5–6; Appendix A, p. 8
column11: Full coverage because node impersonation is explicitly described, mitigated and demonstrated. The mechanism relies on source IP addresses rather than cryptographic identity, which remains a documented limitation.

column2: ROSMonitoring: A Runtime Verification Framework for ROS
column7: The paper defines application-level behavioral properties over ROS messages and evaluates them using a simulated Mars Curiosity rover. The monitor intercepts commands on the wheels_control topic and checks whether turning commands exceed speed 10 or forward/backward commands exceed speed 15. Messages violating the property are discarded before reaching the rover controller, preventing unsafe high-speed turns that could cause the rover to roll over or crash.
column8: Sec. 2, pp. 4–11; Sec. 3.1, pp. 11–13; Listing 3 and Curiosity property specification
column11: Primary code. The fault is a violation of an author-defined behavioral and domain-safety property. No lower-level programming, communication configuration or scheduling root cause is established.

column2: ROS-Defender: SDN-Based Security Policy Enforcement for Robotic Applications
column7: The paper states that ROS topics and services have no effective access control beyond message-type compatibility, allowing arbitrary nodes to join topics, publish forged messages or directly establish connections outside the expected ROS graph. ROSDN maintains mappings among nodes, topics, services, ports and network flows, translates ROS-Policy-Language rules into OpenFlow rules and filters unauthorized connections at the SDN layer.
column8: Sec. I–II, pp. 114–115; Sec. IV-A–D, pp. 116–117; Figs. 1–3
column11: Primary code. Topic- and service-level authorization is directly implemented. The evaluation confirms that the policy-enforcement infrastructure runs on physical and virtual ROS systems, although it does not report a systematic unauthorized-publishing attack suite.

column2: ROS-Defender: SDN-Based Security Policy Enforcement for Robotic Applications
column7: The paper identifies denial of service and compromised-node traffic as gaps in existing ROS and SROS protection. ROSWatch profiles traffic volume, publishing rate, dropping rate, message age and activity duration, while ROS-Policy-Language supports bandwidth limits through OpenFlow meter tables and can drop traffic above configured thresholds.
column8: Sec. I, p. 114; Sec. IV-A, C–D, pp. 116–118
column11: Flow-rate controls and traffic anomaly rules are implemented, but no dedicated DoS or publisher-flood attack experiment, detection rate or false-positive analysis is reported.

column2: ROS-Defender: SDN-Based Security Policy Enforcement for Robotic Applications
column7: The ROS attacker model states that network messages have no authentication, allowing an attacker to impersonate nodes, ROS Master or Parameter Server and spoof connections from arbitrary addresses. ROS-Defender correlates ROS graph state with observed ports and network flows and can block connections from nodes that do not comply with policy.
column8: Sec. III, p. 116; Sec. IV-A–B, pp. 116–117
column11: The paper directly analyzes impersonation, but ROS-Defender does not introduce cryptographic node authentication. Its enforcement depends on ROS Master state, network observations and, where enabled, SROS certificates.

column2: ROS-Defender: SDN-Based Security Policy Enforcement for Robotic Applications
column7: The paper explicitly states that ordinary ROS node-to-node, node-to-Master and node-to-Parameter-Server communication is unencrypted and can be observed, intercepted or modified. ROS-Policy-Language can check whether traffic appears encrypted using entropy estimation, and ROS-Defender can operate together with SROS/TLS, but it does not itself encrypt ROS traffic.
column8: Sec. I–III, pp. 114–116; Sec. IV-D, pp. 117–118
column11: The confidentiality defect is analyzed, but the proposed system primarily monitors or enforces whether encryption is present rather than supplying an independent encryption protocol.

column2: Towards a Robotic Intrusion Prevention System: Combining Security and Safety in Cognitive Social Robots
column7: The proposed RIPS rule language can inspect the number and identity of publishers and subscribers associated with a ROS 2 topic. Functions such as publishers, publishersinclude, topicpublishers and topicpublishersinclude allow the system to detect a publisher that is not part of the expected ROS 2 computation graph. RIPS may then issue an alert, execute a filtering program or transition the robot to a more restrictive System Mode.
column8: Sec. 4.3–4.4, pp. 5–6; Sec. 5, pp. 6–8; Figs. 1 and 3
column11: Primary code. The capability directly addresses unexpected or impersonated publishers on shared topics, but no forged-publisher or publisher-impersonation attack is executed. The experimental RIPS core is emulated.

column2: Towards a Robotic Intrusion Prevention System: Combining Security and Safety in Cognitive Social Robots
column7: The paper explicitly states that a RIPS rule can maintain a message counter together with the current time to detect flooding attacks. Its action model can execute an external firewall or filtering program, increase the alert level and switch the robot to a restricted or halted operating mode.
column11: Flooding detection and mitigation are explicit design capabilities, but the evaluation contains no authenticated-node flooding experiment, traffic-rate benchmark, detection accuracy or false-positive measurement.

column2: Watch Your Callback: Offline Anomaly Detection Using Machine Learning in ROS 2
column7: The method directly monitors callback response time and invocation frequency as indicators of abnormal execution. In the evaluation, the authors modify the callbackJointState callback by injecting delays of 10–100 ms and 500–1000 ms, shortening its normal 500 ms interval to 100–200 ms, or extending it to 900–1000 ms. Isolation Forest, OCSVM and Autoencoder are then evaluated on detecting these temporal callback deviations.
column8: Sec. III-C–D, pp. 60766–60767; Sec. IV-B–F, pp. 60767–60771; Fig. 4; Table 1; Tables 3–5
column11: Primary code. The directly manipulated and measured defect locus is callback execution timing. Coverage does not establish the prevalence of real ROS 2 executor faults because the cases are author-created.

column2: Watch Your Callback: Offline Anomaly Detection Using Machine Learning in ROS 2
column7: The four malicious scenarios are designed to emulate direct and indirect DoS behavior. The burst scenario increases callback invocation frequency to represent Ping of Death or SYN flooding, while the response-time and delayed-frequency scenarios emulate RUDY, Slowloris and related service-degradation attacks.
column11: Partial because the experiments perturb a callback directly; they do not implement an authenticated DDS publisher or service client, nor separately demonstrate that missing throttling or backpressure permits the attack.

column2: Intrusion Detection on Robot Cameras Using Spatio-Temporal Autoencoders: A Self-Driving Car Application
column7: The attack model allows a fake node to publish to the camera image topic and to intercept, inject, modify or replay camera frames. The evaluated cases include black or white frame insertion, past-image replay, image blurring, object concealment and modification of a traffic light from red to green. The proposed detector is directly evaluated on all ten attack scenarios.
column8: Sec. I-A, p. 1; Sec. II, p. 2; Fig. 1; Table I; Sec. IV-D, pp. 4–5
column11: Primary code. The direct defect mechanism is unauthorized publication and alteration of data on a ROS topic. Object misclassification is the resulting impact rather than a BSE fault.

column2: Intrusion Detection on Robot Cameras Using Spatio-Temporal Autoencoders: A Self-Driving Car Application
column7: Scenarios 5 and 6 inject multiple successive duplicate or black images to flood the image-processing node. These flooding sequences are included in the experimental dataset and evaluated using the reconstruction model.
column8: Sec. II, p. 2; Table I; Fig. 2; Sec. IV-D, p. 5; Fig. 6
column11: Directly evaluated malicious message flooding. The paper does not implement rate limiting, queue control or mitigation; it detects the resulting anomalous frames.

column2: Intrusion Detection on Robot Cameras Using Spatio-Temporal Autoencoders: A Self-Driving Car Application
column7: The adversarial model assumes that an attacker can create a fake ROS node and insert it between the camera publisher and image-processing subscriber. However, the paper does not separately test malicious registration, duplicate node identity, certificate validation or authentication bypass.
column8: Sec. I-A, p. 1; Sec. II, p. 2; Fig. 1
column11: The fake node is part of the assumed attack model, while the evaluation operates on already perturbed image sequences. Therefore, node authentication receives Partial rather than Full.

column2: Intrusion Detection on Robot Cameras Using Spatio-Temporal Autoencoders: A Self-Driving Car Application
column7: The paper states that ROS node communication lacks protection and may allow attackers to learn confidential information or conduct a man-in-the-middle attack. Nevertheless, the proposed detector neither analyzes plaintext network traffic nor implements encryption.
column8: Sec. I-A–B, p. 1
column11: Lack of communication confidentiality is explicitly discussed but is not part of the experimental evaluation.

column2: Detecting Data Injection Attacks in ROS Systems Using Machine Learning
column7: The paper explicitly defines the studied attack as unauthorized publishing. The attacker invokes publisherUpdate on the /gazebo subscriber, adds a fake publisher named /turtlebot3_false, and injects incorrect movement messages into /cmd_vel in parallel with the legitimate /turtlebot3_drive publisher. The resulting network traffic is used to train and evaluate the SVM detector.
column8: Sec. III-B, p. 225; Sec. IV-A–B, pp. 226–227; Figs. 2, 4 and 5
column11: Primary code. This is a directly implemented and evaluated topic-injection attack. The resulting unpredictable movement and collision risk are secondary functional impacts.

column2: Detecting Data Injection Attacks in ROS Systems Using Machine Learning
column7: The paper states that ROS nodes do not need to identify or authenticate themselves before acting and that the ROS Master cannot enforce a mapping between topics and legitimate nodes. The experiment uses a fake ROS node, but it does not separately evaluate duplicate-node registration, identity impersonation, certificate validation or authentication bypass.
column8: Sec. III-A, pp. 224–225; Sec. IV-A, p. 227
column11: Authentication absence is an explicit enabling condition, but the evaluated mechanism is unauthorized publishing rather than a distinct node-authentication experiment.

column2: Trusted Operations of a Military Ground Robot in the Face of Man-in-the-Middle Cyberattacks Using Deep Learning Convolutional Neural Networks: Real-Time Experimental Outcomes
column7: ROS 1 allows nodes to participate in open topics without adequate authorization. In the evaluated attack, RosPenTo is used to compromise the /cmd_vel control topic: legitimate commands from /jaus_mobility are overwritten by unintended traffic originating from /gvrbot_imu_filter, causing /gvrbot_mobility to receive false control information. The attack is executed in real time on the physical GVR-BOT and is used to construct the malicious training and test data.
column11: Primary code. The experimentally demonstrated mechanism is unauthorized modification and injection of control-topic data.

column2: Trusted Operations of a Military Ground Robot in the Face of Man-in-the-Middle Cyberattacks Using Deep Learning Convolutional Neural Networks: Real-Time Experimental Outcomes
column7: The paper identifies ROS 1’s anonymous graph structure, lack of payload-authenticity verification, and inability to identify malicious participants as enabling conditions for the attack. However, it does not separately evaluate node registration impersonation, duplicate node names, certificates, challenge-response authentication, or authentication bypass.
column11: Authentication weakness is explicit, but the experimental case focuses on control-topic traffic replacement rather than a distinct node-authentication attack.

column2: Trusted Operations of a Military Ground Robot in the Face of Man-in-the-Middle Cyberattacks Using Deep Learning Convolutional Neural Networks: Real-Time Experimental Outcomes
column7: The paper explicitly states that ROS 1 network traffic is unencrypted, allowing attackers to eavesdrop, record or manipulate data and conduct man-in-the-middle attacks. Nevertheless, the experimental outcome is command-data replacement rather than a separately measured confidentiality breach, packet-decryption experiment or intercepted sensitive-data case.
column11: Plaintext communication is an explicit enabling weakness, but confidentiality loss is not independently evaluated.

column2: DCWM-LSTM: A Novel Attack Detection Framework for Robotic Arms
column7: In the replay scenario, an attacker creates and registers a ROS node, requests information about the target publisher, subscribes to the target data, records two minutes of legitimate data and then continuously republishes the recorded data to the robotic system. The attack is implemented against the physical robotic-arm environment and directly evaluated using the resulting joint-position and velocity traces.
column11: Primary code. Replay is an unauthorized ROS data-access and republication operation. Its principal consequence is replacement of current system information with previously valid data.

column2: DCWM-LSTM: A Novel Attack Detection Framework for Robotic Arms
column7: In the subscriber-flood scenario, the attacker sends multiple consecutive subscription requests to ROS-Master. ROS-Master then attempts to process and propagate the requests, leading to Master overload or crash, delays in robotic-arm movements and temporary loss of responsiveness. Three one-minute flooding periods are injected and evaluated in the physical testbed.
column11: Directly implemented ROS-specific DoS case. The authors report that the arm remained unresponsive for approximately four minutes after the second attack.

column2: DCWM-LSTM: A Novel Attack Detection Framework for Robotic Arms
column7: Both attack scenarios rely on an attacker being able to create and register a node with ROS-Master without authentication. The paper also explicitly states that ROS lacks the authentication mechanisms required for basic access control. However, it does not separately test node-name impersonation, certificate validation, registration authentication or identity-binding mechanisms.
column8: Sec. I, p. 20548; Sec. III-A, p. 20551
column11: Lack of node authentication is an explicit enabling condition, but the evaluated attack objectives are replay and flooding rather than authentication bypass itself.

column2: ROZZ: Property-based Fuzzing for Robotic Programs in ROS
column7: ROZZ directly detects 43 real bugs in ten ROS 2 programs: six null-pointer dereferences, five use-after-free defects, three buffer or stack overflows, eleven invalid-pointer accesses and eighteen uncaught exceptions. Root-cause analysis attributes confirmed bugs to callback data races and incorrect synchronization, missing or incorrect validation and exception handling, and stack-memory misuse. Twenty bugs were confirmed and fixed by ROS developers. The ROS 1 evaluation additionally finds two invalid-pointer accesses and four uncaught exceptions.
column8: Sec. IV-A–B, pp. 6788–6790; Tables II–III; Fig. 6; Sec. IV-D, p. 6790; Table V
column11: Primary and only supported leaf code. Most defects cause node crashes or abnormal termination of robot tasks; some memory-safety defects may also cause undefined robot behavior or create security risk.

column2: Multi-Dimensional and Message-Guided Fuzzing for Robotic Programs in Robot Operating System
column7: ROFER finds 88 real implementation defects across 13 ROS 2 programs: 10 null-pointer dereferences, 8 use-after-free defects, 14 buffer or stack overflows, 17 invalid-pointer accesses and 39 unhandled exceptions. Root-cause analysis shows defects involving harmful data races during message handling, missing synchronization, incorrect handling of configuration parameters, missing or incorrect safety checks, and improper exception handling. Forty-six bugs were confirmed by ROS developers.
column11: Primary and only supported leaf code. The observed consequences include initialization failure, loss of response, abnormal stopping, collision and incorrect task completion.

column2: Toward the Trustworthiness of Industrial Robotics Using Differential Fuzz Testing
column7: RROSFuzz supplies identical six-joint target-angle arrays to the Python moveit_commander and C++ move_group_interface implementations. Approximately 60.78% of the 15,246 test cases produce inconsistent end-effector positions or orientations. Validation using final joint-angle values shows that 74.56% of inconsistent cases are closer to the result of move_group_interface. The authors attribute the discrepancy to joint-angle overflow or incorrect angle handling in moveit_commander.arm.go(), which can prevent the arm from reaching the specified target and may cause obstacle collision.

column11: Primary and only supported leaf code. The defect is identified through inconsistent robot-motion semantics rather than a crash, memory-safety violation or ROS communication failure.

column2: RoboFuzz: Fuzzing Robotic Systems over Robot Operating System (ROS) for Finding Correctness Bugs
column7: The paper directly defines and evaluates three semantic-correctness families: violations of physical laws, violations of robot specifications, and cyber-physical discrepancies. RoboFuzz detects specification and behavioral faults in PX4, TurtleBot3, MoveIt 2, and Turtlesim, including unconstrained acceleration, incorrect motor and joint limits, inconsistent simulated and physical behavior, zero velocity reported during movement, and physically infeasible states.

column11: Primary code. The defects were triggered with concrete messages, replayed for validation, and many were acknowledged or fixed by developers.

column2: RoboFuzz: Fuzzing Robotic Systems over Robot Operating System (ROS) for Finding Correctness Bugs
column7: RoboFuzz directly discovers implementation-level defects in ROSIDL, rclpy, rclcpp, and application controllers, including type confusion, missing range and type validation, implicit value conversion, incorrect return logic, missing NULL checks causing null-pointer dereference, unhandled exceptions, and unreachable error-checking code.

column2: RoboFuzz: Fuzzing Robotic Systems over Robot Operating System (ROS) for Finding Correctness Bugs
column7: Table 2 reports an acknowledged mismatch in the PX4 trajectory-setpoint message definition. This is a direct ROS message-interface contract defect rather than merely an incorrect downstream behavior.

column2: DiscoFuzzer: Discontinuity-based Vulnerability Detector for Robotic Systems
column7: DiscoFuzzer treats discontinuous or unexpected changes in robotic outputs as correctness anomalies. It calculates first and second derivatives, checks whether past inputs improperly dominate current states, and detects output fields that change contrary to their normal input–output relationships. The motivating example detects uncontrolled rapid joint rotation caused by failure to enforce a physical constraint. Its discontinuity analysis detected 63 distinct issues, including six previously unknown issues.
column8: Abstract; Sec. 2 and Fig. 1, pp. 2–4; Sec. 4.2, pp. 6–7; Sec. 5.3 and Fig. 4, p. 9
column11: Primary code. The method directly targets violations of physical continuity and expected robotic behavior. The paper calls these findings vulnerabilities, but the evaluated root cause is primarily internal behavioral correctness rather than missing authorization or another security policy.

column2: DiscoFuzzer: Discontinuity-based Vulnerability Detector for Robotic Systems
column7: The paper explicitly discusses memory-overflow effects, floating-point calculation errors, division values tending toward infinity, propagation of NaN/infinity and process crashes. DiscoFuzzer includes a separate crash detector, which identified 22 distinct issues. However, the paper does not describe the implementation root cause of each detected benchmark issue, so crashes alone are insufficient for Full GPE coverage.

column2: Enhancing ROS System Fuzzing through Callback Tracing
column7: R2D2 discovered 39 previously unknown implementation defects: 23 memory-related defects and 16 concurrency-related defects. Table 1 explicitly reports OOM, buffer overflows, use-after-free, segmentation faults, double-free, null-pointer dereferences, memory leaks, data races, and deadlocks in ROS 2 runtime components and applications. Eight defects were confirmed and six were fixed.

column11: Primary code. Generic races and deadlocks are classified as GPE under the manual unless their root cause is specifically an executor, callback-group, queue, or scheduling configuration fault.

column2: Enhancing ROS System Fuzzing through Callback Tracing
column7: The paper analyzes a ROS executor scheduling fault in which low- and high-priority mutex operations share wait_mutex_, delaying timer insertion and producing irregular callback timing. R2D2 consequently monitors callback execution latency, scheduling latency, callback ordering, and message throughput as indicators of runtime state. However, the evaluated 39 new defects are reported mainly as memory and generic concurrency bugs rather than as a separately validated scheduling-fault category.
column8: Sec. 3 and Fig. 2, pp. 78–79; Secs. 4.1–4.2 and Figs. 4–6, pp. 80–81
column11: Partial because the executor-scheduling fault is an externally existing ROS issue used to motivate the approach; the paper does not establish timing or scheduling fault detection as an independently evaluated output category.

column2: Property-Based Testing for the Robot Operating System
column7: The paper identifies ROS component orchestration as a common source of bugs: developers must use configuration files, topic and service names, namespaces, launch files, and remappings to ensure that nodes communicate through the intended interfaces. The proposed generator extracts the computation graph with HAROS, identifies open input and output topics, generates matching publishers and subscribers, and checks that the runtime ROS interface remains stable.

column11: Primary code. The method directly verifies node/topic integration and expected computation-graph structure. The evidence is primarily an implemented architectural property rather than a reported real-world misconfiguration.

column2: Property-Based Testing for the Robot Operating System
column7: The generated tests support user-defined behavioral, historical, and temporal contracts relating received messages to expected outputs. In the Kobuki experiment, the authors specify a safety-controller property connecting bumper, cliff and wheel-drop sensor states to velocity commands; Hypothesis automatically generates a minimal message sequence that falsifies the property.

column2: Property-Based Testing for the Robot Operating System
column7: The test framework attempts to generate message sequences that crash a configuration and includes a default liveness property requiring all tested nodes to remain alive and responsive. However, the preliminary evaluation does not report a concrete crash, exception, memory error, or source-level implementation defect.

column2: Checking consistency of robot software architectures in ROS
column7: ROS nodes connect implicitly through named topics and services. Incorrect launch configuration can therefore create disconnected components, unintended connections, missing publishers, incorrect remappings, or incompatible topic and service relationships. The proposed tool reconstructs the expected ROS graph from launch files and sandboxed node execution, and reports publishers and subscribers so that inconsistencies such as subscribed but unpublished topics can be detected.
column8: Abstract; Sec. 1.1, pp. 1–2; Sec. 3 and Fig. 1, p. 3; Sec. 3.5, p. 6; Sec. 4, Tables 1–3, pp. 6–7

column2: Static-time Extraction and Analysis of the ROS Computation Graph
column7: The paper directly targets ROS orchestration and interface consistency. Its queries detect publisher/subscriber message-type mismatches, disconnected topics with similar names, missing or incorrect name remappings, problematic global ROS names, conditional endpoints, and whether nodes are connected transitively to the robot base. The authors report that use of global ROS names was an actual issue in AgRob V16 and that the tool helped correct it.
column8: Abstract and Sec. I, pp. 62–63; Sec. III-C, pp. 65–66; Sec. IV-B and Figs. 9–10, pp. 67–68

column2: Static-time Extraction and Analysis of the ROS Computation Graph
column7: The query catalogue checks for unbounded message queues and queues of size one. The paper explains that unbounded queues may exhaust memory, while size-one queues may cause message loss. Several size-one queues were observed in AgRob V16, mainly in third-party packages, but the study did not execute experiments showing actual queue overflow, missed deadlines, or runtime failure.

column11: Partial because risky queue configurations are explicitly identified, but their runtime consequences are not directly evaluated.

column2: Verification of System-Wide Safety Properties of ROS Applications
column7: The method directly verifies behavioral and domain-semantic safety properties relating sensor messages, operating modes, command values and actuator behavior. In AgRob V16, model checking showed that the property requiring in-place rotation during autonomous path-following to be justified by laser obstacle detection did not hold: accumulated localization errors could cause the PathPlanner to issue a rotation command even though no laser obstacle message existed.
column8: Abstract; Sec. II and Figs. 5–8, pp. 7249–7250; Sec. IV, Figs. 14–15 and Table I, pp. 7253–7254
column11: Primary code. The property was developed with AgRob V16 domain experts and a concrete counterexample was produced by bounded model checking. Because the issue was not independently reproduced at runtime, the evidence establishes property coverage rather than real-world defect prevalence.

column2: A Framework for Quality Assessment of ROS Repositories
column7: HAROS performs static analysis of ROS source repositories and reports source-code quality metrics, quality-threshold violations and violations of C++ coding standards. Its plug-ins wrap tools such as Cppcheck and roslint and support approximately 120 coding rules. Evaluation on 180 ROS packages identified overly complex, tightly coupled and insufficiently documented code, together with large numbers of ROS C++ coding-standard violations.
column8: Abstract and Sec. I, pp. 1–2; Sec. IV-C and Table I, pp. 4–5; Sec. V and Table II, pp. 5–6; Sec. VI, p. 6
