column2: ROSInfer: Statically Inferring Behavioral Component Models for ROS-based Robotics Systems
column7: The paper defines behavioral architectural composition bugs as failures caused by inconsistent component composition and manifested through inter-component communication. In the motivating Autoware.AI case, lattice_trajectory_gen requires an odom_pose input before it can periodically publish its output, but no component sends the required message, causing the component to wait indefinitely. ROSInfer recovered the required trigger and detected this defect, together with autoware-03 and autoware-10, whose important behaviors also depended on required inputs not connected to publishers.
column8: Sec. 1, pp. 1–2; Sec. 2.3 and Figs. 1–2, p. 3; Sec. 5.3, pp. 10–11
column11: Primary code. The behavior model exposes that an input is required, but the underlying fault is a missing publisher–subscriber connection or missing endpoint in the system composition, which falls under ICF.

column2: Towards Automatic Inference of Behavioral Component Models for ROS-Based Robotics Systems
column7: The paper identifies behavioral architectural composition bugs arising when ROS components make undocumented assumptions about initialization messages, internal states, input-output causality or publication frequency. ROSInfer reconstructs reactive, periodic and state-dependent component behavior from ROS API calls, state variables and control flow. It was evaluated on five real-world ROS systems comprising 534 components, using 155 manually constructed behavioral models as ground truth, and reports precision and recall for periodic, reactive and state-dependent behavior. The inferred models have already enabled the automatic detection of three real-world bugs.
column8: Sec. 1, p. 1; Sec. 2.1 and Fig. 1, p. 2; Sec. 2.2, p. 3; Sec. 2.4, p. 4
column11: Full because behavioral composition defects are the direct research object and the completed static-analysis component is empirically evaluated. The proposed injected-bug and developer-study evaluations are not counted as completed evidence.

column2: Lightweight Detection of Physical Unit Inconsistencies without Program Annotations
column7: The study defines unit inconsistencies as operations that violate physical dimensional semantics, including assigning meters to a meters-per-second field, comparing linear and angular velocity, and adding force-derived and torque-derived quantities. Its static-analysis tool propagates units from ROS shared message libraries and detects inconsistent assignment, addition and comparison. Evaluation on 213 ROS systems found inconsistencies in 24 systems, with an 87% true-positive rate for high-confidence findings.
column8: Abstract and Sec. 1, pp. 1–2; Sec. 2.2, pp. 3–4; Sec. 3 and Algorithm 1, pp. 3–7; Sec. 5, Tables 2–4, pp. 7–9; Sec. 7, p. 10
column11: Full because physical-unit inconsistency is the direct defect target, the tool is implemented, and defects are detected in real ROS repositories. One reported Romeo robot defect was acknowledged and patched by its developers.

column2: Phriky-Units: A Lightweight, Annotation-Free Physical Unit Inconsistency Detection Tool
column7: Phriky-Units detects three forms of physical-unit semantic inconsistency in ROS C++ programs: addition or subtraction of incompatible units, comparison of incompatible units, and assignment of multiple incompatible units to the same variable. The tool associates ROS message fields with physical units, propagates the units through expressions and reports violations of dimensional-analysis rules. The paper reports 217 findings across 213 projects and an 87% true-positive rate for high-confidence findings.
column8: Abstract and Sec. 1, p. 1; Fig. 2 and Sec. 2, pp. 1–3; Sec. 4, Figs. 4–5, pp. 3–4
column11: Full defect coverage, but the empirical results are reused from the authors’ longer companion paper rather than generated by an independent evaluation in this publication.

column2: Phys: Probabilistic Physical Unit Assignment and Inconsistency Detection
column7: Phys detects violations of physical-unit semantics, including addition or subtraction of incompatible units, comparison of incompatible units, assignments between different units and inconsistent units supplied to the same function argument. It probabilistically infers units from ROS message definitions, dataflow, variable names, mathematical expressions, known symbols and conversion patterns. Evaluation on ROS C++ files shows that Phys infers units for 159.3% more variables than Phriky and detects 103.3% more inconsistencies, while maintaining an overall reported true-positive rate of approximately 85.3%.
column8: Abstract and Sec. 1, pp. 1–2; Sec. 2.1, pp. 2–3; Secs. 3–4 and Figs. 1–3, pp. 3–7; Sec. 5 and Tables 4–7, pp. 7–10
column11: Full because physical-unit inconsistency is the direct defect target, the method is implemented and real inconsistencies are identified in public ROS software. The expanded evaluation reports 156 true-positive inconsistencies in 45 files, compared with 75 found by Phriky.

column2: PhysFrame: Type Checking Physical Frames of Reference for Robotic Systems
column7: PhysFrame models physical frames and transformations as types and detects violations involving incorrect transform values, axis-orientation conventions, transform directions, and physical-frame semantics. The motivating ORB-SLAM2 case omits the final conversion from RDF back to ROS FLU orientation, producing a transform that can cause downstream robot misbehavior. The evaluation directly reports incorrect-transform findings and violations of common frame conventions.
column11: Primary code. Although the defect is implemented in C/C++ code, the root cause is incorrect physical and coordinate-frame semantics, so it is BSE rather than GPE.

column2: PhysFrame: Type Checking Physical Frames of Reference for Robotic Systems
column7: PhysFrame explicitly detects malformed relationships and configuration bindings among ROS frames, including multiple parents or cycles in the TF tree, incorrect TF-tree ordering, missing frame or child-frame identifiers, redundant transforms, and reversed transform naming. These faults are directly evaluated on 180 public ROS projects, and several findings were fixed or acknowledged by developers.
column11: Independent secondary defect family. These cases concern frame relationships, identifiers, TF-tree contracts, and launch/source configuration rather than the physical values of the transformation.

column2: SA4U: Practical Static Analysis for Unit Type Error Detection
column7: SA4U detects unit-type errors involving incompatible physical units, scale differences within the same dimension, and mismatched reference frames. Examples include subtracting meters from centimeters, confusing microseconds with other timestamp representations, and processing coordinates expressed in an unsupported reference frame. Evaluation on ArduPilot and PX4 identified 14 previously unknown errors and detected five of six selected historical errors.
column8: Abstract and Sec. 1, pp. 1–2; Sec. 2 and Figs. 1–3, pp. 2–4; Secs. 3–4 and Fig. 4, pp. 4–7; Sec. 5 and Tables 3–6, pp. 7–9; Sec. 6, pp. 9–10
column11: Full defect coverage in the broader robotic-software domain, but not direct evidence about ROS. Fourteen newly reported bugs constitute EP-OBS; the six previously known bugs provide additional historical validation.

column2: UPPAAL-Based Modeling and Verification of ROS 2 Multi-threaded Execution and Operating System Reservations
column7: The study directly models and verifies ROS 2 multi-threaded executor scheduling, callback-group mutual exclusion, ready-set resetting, callback blocking, starvation risk, and delays introduced by underlying OS reservations. Experiments show that using two mutually exclusive executor threads can produce higher callback latency than one thread; lower-priority callbacks may be repeatedly blocked by newly released higher-priority callbacks, potentially leading to starvation. UPPAAL timed-automata templates calculate worst-case callback latency and reproduce the observed ROS 2 execution traces.
column8: Sec. 1, PDF pp. 4–5; Secs. 3.3–3.5, PDF pp. 11–15; Sec. 4.2, PDF pp. 16–18, Figs. 8–9 and Tables 1–2; Secs. 4.3–4.4, PDF pp. 18–20, Fig. 10
column11: The strongest evidence is the callback-latency and execution-order behavior observed in real ROS 2 test-system traces. The operating-system reservation extension is evaluated using synthetic traces and manual calculations, so that part has weaker independent grounding. Do not assign a vulnerability code merely because the paper uses the word “vulnerabilities”; the root cause is ROS executor scheduling and runtime execution behavior.

column2: A Model-Based Methodology for Automated Verification of ROS 2 Systems
column7: The methodology explicitly targets ROS 2 executor-related timing and execution faults, particularly callback blocking, excessive callback latency, insufficient input-buffer capacity, buffer overflow, and missed callback instances. It derives callback release times, execution times, periods, and buffer sizes from ROS2_tracing, transforms them through Eclipse metamodels, and generates UPPAAL models intended to verify these properties. However, the proof-of-concept evaluation primarily validates trace extraction, model transformations, and generation of executable UPPAAL code; it does not present a directly evaluated fault-triggering case or a demonstrated latency/buffer property violation in the studied example.
column8: Abstract, PDF p. 1; Sec. 1.1, PDF p. 2; Secs. 2.3–2.4, PDF p. 3; Secs. 3.1–3.2 and Figs. 3–4, PDF pp. 4–6; Sec. 4.2, PDF p. 7; Sec. 6, PDF pp. 7–8
column11: Partial, rather than Full, because the paper directly proposes automation for SEF verification but does not independently demonstrate an actual callback-blocking, buffer-overflow, or missed-instance defect in its proof-of-concept evaluation. The concrete defect evidence is largely inherited from the authors’ earlier executor studies and UPPAAL templates.

column2: Formal Verification of ROS-based Robotic Applications using Timed-Automata
column7: The paper directly studies faults caused by ROS queue sizes, publisher rates, subscriber spin rates, callback execution times, communication delays, and callback timeouts. UPPAAL verification shows that unsuitable parameter combinations cause publisher or subscriber queue overflow. In the Kobuki case study, overflow can replace safety-critical sensor messages before they are processed, while priority and timeout configurations can prevent RandomWalker velocity commands from ever reaching the robot motor.
column8: Sec. IV-A–C, pp. 46–47; Sec. V-A–C, pp. 47–50; Table I, p. 48; Figs. 5–6, pp. 48–50
column11: Primary and only defect code. The violations are demonstrated through author-defined safety and liveness properties over timed-automata models. They are not validated through physical robot execution.

column2: Pattern-based verification of ROS 2 applications using UPPAAL
column7: The paper directly verifies faults arising from ROS 2 executor scheduling, callback execution latency, callback blocking, and insufficient input or output buffer sizes. A buffer overflow causes callback instances or messages to be missed. In SC2, the model checker detects a buffer overflow under ExV2, and the result corresponds to the actual ROS 2 execution. The approach also computes worst-case callback latency and generates counterexample traces for potentially problematic scheduling paths. SC3 separately demonstrates output-buffer overflow under different buffer sizes, delays, and jitter values.
column11: The evaluated scenarios are author-constructed ROS 2 benchmark configurations. SC1 and SC2 are additionally checked against actual ROS 2 execution traces, but the fault-triggering configurations remain synthetic experimental cases.

column2: Verifying ROS-Based Applications Using Timed and Stochastic Timed Automata
column7: The paper directly analyzes ROS scheduling and execution faults involving callback/task priorities, processing windows, periodic and subscription-triggered jobs, WCET/BCET variation, task queues and probabilistic system load. It verifies the maximum end-to-end reaction time from sensor release to actuator completion. The analysis shows that variable execution times may counterintuitively increase the worst-case reaction time, and that increasing the number or load of camera-processing chains can cause the required reaction-time bound of 850 time units to be violated.
column11: Primary and only defect code. Deadline violations and maximum-reaction-time properties are defined and evaluated over author-created formal models. Validation against the previously published simulation benchmark supports semantic consistency, but does not establish that the modeled deadline violations occurred in a deployed ROS 2 system.

column2: DiNeROS: A Model-Driven Framework for Verifiable ROS Applications with Petri Nets
column7: DiNeROS explicitly models the bounded outgoing publisher queue, node-level dispatcher queue, and subscriber callback queue. Overflow transitions are inserted into the flattened Petri net and checked through reachability analysis. In the case study, increasing the number of objects without consistently adjusting queue capacities causes controller-side overflow; another configuration causes the user-interface callback queue to overflow when communication is delayed.
column8: Sec. II, p. 792; Sec. V-C and V-E, pp. 795–797; Sec. VI-A.1–A.2, p. 798; Figs. 5 and 9
column11: Primary code. The faults are constructed by changing object counts, queue capacities, and communication conditions in the case-study model. Queue overflow and callback-message loss belong to SEF rather than ICF.

column2: DiNeROS: A Model-Driven Framework for Verifiable ROS Applications with Petri Nets
column7: The evaluation introduces an input condition Danger ∧ ¬Danger, which permanently disables the associated transition and makes the unsafe state unreachable after initialization. A second condition makes PickSuccess constantly false, preventing the pick service from returning and thereby blocking all robots. Both faults are detected through reachability and LTL analysis of the Petri-net model.
column11: Independent secondary fault family. The root cause is an invalid behavioral condition or workflow predicate, not a ROS interface or generic source-code error.

column2: Distributed Petri Nets for Model-Driven Verifiable Robotic Applications in ROS
column7: The paper directly models and verifies structural and communication relationships among ROS nodes, topics, services, publishers, subscribers, clients, and servers. Its Net Analyzer searches Petri-net state spaces for publisher, dispatcher, and subscriber queue overflow; unused topic channels; services that are never called or never return; and nodes whose transitions are all dead. In the evaluated scenario, developers add two new object types and modify publisher-side capacities without correspondingly increasing the subscriber-side capacity. DiNeROS reaches a state in which the topic overflow transition is enabled, thereby detecting the inconsistent communication configuration.
column8: Secs. 5.3–5.5, journal pp. 539–545 / PDF pp. 9–15; Sec. 7.1 and Algorithms 1–3, journal pp. 548–549 / PDF pp. 18–19; Sec. 9.2.1, journal p. 552 / PDF p. 22
column11: ICF, rather than SEF, because the demonstrated overflow originates from inconsistent topic-channel capacity configuration across communicating components. It is not caused by a long-running callback, executor scheduling, or runtime queue starvation. The defect scenario is deliberately constructed by the authors.

column2: Distributed Petri Nets for Model-Driven Verifiable Robotic Applications in ROS
column7: The study directly evaluates invalid behavioral and logical conditions in the Petri-net workflow. An unsatisfiable condition such as Danger ∧ ¬Danger permanently disables the associated transition and prevents the safety model from returning to the unsafe state. A second example makes ICPickSuccess constantly false, preventing the pick service from returning and blocking the robots. In the case-study scenario, changing the sensor signal clause to an unsatisfiable expression causes the Sensor and Pick services never to return, the Place service never to be called, the UI topic to remain unused, and ultimately blocks the complete application.
column8: Sec. 7.2, journal p. 549 / PDF p. 19; Sec. 9.2.2, journal p. 552 / PDF p. 22
column11: The root cause is an unsatisfiable domain or workflow condition, not incorrect ROS endpoint wiring. Therefore, this distinct fault family is coded as BSE. The downstream service and topic failures are consequences of the invalid behavioral condition and should not be counted again as separate ICF instances for this scenario.

column2: Formal Verification of ROS Based Systems Using a Linear Logic Theorem Prover
column7: The study directly verifies ROS computational-graph consistency and compatibility properties, including idle publishers and subscribers, publisher–subscriber type consistency, multiple publishers to the same topic, compatibility of newly added components, and whether the graph can realize a required behavior. In the evaluated bad design, the authors remove the cmd_vel_mux node and connect velocity outputs from both kobuki_keyop and kobuki_safety_controller directly to the mobile-base velocity topic. The theorem prover cannot prove the original single-command behavior property, exposing an architectural interaction flaw that may result in unpredictable robot behavior.
column8: Sec. I, PDF p. 1; Sec. IV-A, PDF pp. 3–4, Figs. 2–5; Sec. IV-B, PDF pp. 4–5, Figs. 6–7
column11: ICF is preferred over BSE for this fault instance because its earliest root cause is the removal of an arbitration component and the resulting incorrect relationship among publishers, topic, and subscriber. The unpredictable motion is the consequence, not the root-cause category.

column2: Formal Verification of ROS Based Systems Using a Linear Logic Theorem Prover
column7: The dynamic verification experiment encodes three behavioral safety rules that classify which combinations of bumper, wheel-drop, and cliff sensor states are acceptable. The authors inject a stuck-on fault into the center bumper signal. After the simulated robot collides, it cannot recover and moves incorrectly; the sensor monitor marks the signal as faulty, the linear-logic verifier determines that the weakest safety rule is no longer satisfied, and the system disables the robot by unloading the velocity multiplexer. This is a distinct behavioral-property and sensor-semantics fault family.
column8: Sec. V-A, PDF pp. 4–5, Figs. 8–9; Sec. V-B, PDF pp. 5–6, definitions of SR1–SR3; Sec. V-C, PDF p. 6
column11: The injected sensor fault is coded BSE because verification is based on explicit domain and behavioral safety constraints over sensor meanings. The monitor and shutdown response are detection and mitigation mechanisms. The authors explicitly describe this experiment as a proof of concept rather than a certified functional-safety system.

column2: Formal Analysis and Detection for ROS2 Communication Security Vulnerability
column7: In the SROS2 experiment, unauthenticated attacker nodes are blocked, whereas attacker nodes that have become authorized can successfully execute all seven topic, service, and action attacks. The authors attribute this result to the absence of a reliable mechanism for remotely transmitting SROS2 security profiles: intercepted profiles can be reused to achieve identity authentication and gain communication privileges.
column11: Primary code. The experiment directly analyzes insufficient protection of SROS2 security profiles and the resulting authenticated privilege abuse.

column2: Formal Analysis and Detection for ROS2 Communication Security Vulnerability
column7: ROS2Tester obtains the target topic name and type, creates a malicious publisher in the same communication domain, constructs a forged message, and publishes it to the target topic. All subscribers receive the false message. The attack succeeds in default ROS 2 and also succeeds against SROS2 when the attacker has an authorized identity.
column11: Independent secondary code. The experiment demonstrates that messages on a shared topic are accepted from a malicious publisher without reliable binding to the intended legitimate source.

column2: ROSCallBaX: Statically Detecting Inconsistencies in Callback Function Setup of Robotic Systems
column7: ROSCallBaX detects incorrect compositions of callback execution elements, including callback deadlocks, using a single-threaded executor for callbacks intended to execute concurrently, assigning callback groups to incompatible or multiple executors, spinning an executor from multiple threads, spinning from inside callbacks, missing spin operations, multiple blocking spins, unsupported nested spins and callbacks disabled by prematurely destroyed local objects. These faults can prevent callbacks from executing, halt processing, introduce races or deadlocks, and increase response time. The tool detected 92 cases across forum-derived programs and public ROS projects with an 88.04% true-positive rate.
column11: Primary and only defect code. The forum dataset contains reconstructed examples, while the project dataset provides observed inconsistencies in real public ROS code.

column2: A Novel Solution for Securing Robot Communications Based on the MQTT Protocol and ROS
column7: The paper identifies that native ROS communications transmit topic and service data in cleartext over TCP/IP or UDP/IP and therefore permit eavesdropping and interception. The proposed architecture routes remote communication through an MQTT Mosquitto broker configured with TLS and X.509 certificates, providing payload encryption. The authors implement the secured and unsecured configurations on three surveillance robots and measure the resulting connection delay, message throughput, and message rate.
column8: Abstract and Sec. I, PDF p. 1; Sec. III, PDF p. 2; Sec. IV-A–B, PDF pp. 3–4, Fig. 1; Sec. V, PDF pp. 4–5, Tables I–III and Figs. 3–4; Sec. VI, PDF p. 6
column11: Full because encryption is a direct implemented and evaluated component of the method. The performance experiment does not itself prove resistance to eavesdropping, but it directly evaluates the deployed TLS-protected communication architecture. Internal ROS communications remain unencrypted, which the authors acknowledge as a limitation.

column2: A Novel Solution for Securing Robot Communications Based on the MQTT Protocol and ROS
column7: The study explicitly identifies the absence of built-in ROS authentication as a weakness that allows remote, untrusted entities to access robot resources. In the proposed architecture, remote clients must authenticate to the MQTT broker using valid X.509 digital certificates before a secure channel with the robots can be established. The implemented experiments compare communication without authentication and certificates against communication with certificate-based client–server authentication.
column8: Sec. I, PDF p. 1; Sec. II, PDF pp. 1–2; Sec. IV-A–B, PDF p. 3, Fig. 1; Sec. V, PDF p. 4; Sec. VI, PDF p. 6
column11: Full because authentication is not merely recommended: certificate-based authentication is implemented in the evaluated architecture. The paper does not test certificate forgery or authentication bypass, so the evidence demonstrates deployment of the control rather than adversarial robustness.

column2: A Novel Solution for Securing Robot Communications Based on the MQTT Protocol and ROS
column7: The paper states that default ROS access permits clients to publish and subscribe broadly and explains that MQTT Access Control Lists can restrict which clients may access particular topics and which actions they may perform. The architecture also prevents unauthenticated remote clients from directly reaching ROS topics. However, the experiments focus on TLS authentication, encryption, and performance and do not report a concrete ACL policy, an unauthorized publish/subscribe attempt, or topic-level authorization results.
column8: Sec. II, PDF p. 1; Sec. III, PDF p. 2; Sec. IV-A–B, PDF p. 3; Sec. VI, PDF p. 6
column11: Partial because access control is an explicit architectural capability and security objective, but it is not separately instantiated and evaluated with an unauthorized topic or service operation. Authentication alone should not be treated as evidence of fine-grained authorization.

column2: From Models To Software Through Automatic Transformations: An AADL To ROS End-to-End Toolchain
column7: The AADL model represents ROS nodes as processes, node functionality as threads, and publisher–subscriber interaction through typed ports and explicit connections. Connected thread and process ports are required to share the same data type, while topic names, message types, publication rates and node relationships are propagated into the generated ROS implementation. The authors state that use of the approach in an autonomous-wheelchair architecture solved existing design errors and inconsistencies, but the individual defects and validation procedure are not reported.
column8: Sec. II, p. 581; Sec. IV, pp. 581–582; Sec. V, pp. 582–585; Sec. VI, p. 585
column11: Primary code. The mechanism directly maintains consistency among ports, types, topics, connections and generated ROS components, but evidence is primarily a capability and use-case claim.

column2: From Models To Software Through Automatic Transformations: An AADL To ROS End-to-End Toolchain
column7: The generator produces compilation-ready ROS packages containing CMakeLists.txt, package.xml, launch files, executable declarations, custom messages, services and required library dependencies. This automation can prevent missing or inconsistent build and packaging configuration, although the paper does not present a concrete build or dependency fault detected in an experiment.
column8: Abstract, p. 580; Sec. V-B, pp. 583–585; Sec. VI, p. 585
column11: Secondary code. Retain only as Partial because build-fault coverage is inferred from explicit artifact generation rather than demonstrated defect cases.

column2: On the (In)Security of Secure ROS2
column7: The study identifies and experimentally validates two failures in SROS2 credential and policy handling. In V1, SROS2 does not actively revoke old permission files; a malicious robot can retain an expired, correctly signed file and later reload it to recover publish or subscribe privileges that the system owner has revoked. In V2, DDS access-control policies are refreshed only when the corresponding participant or node service is reinitialized, allowing a malicious robot to refuse reinitialization and continue operating under outdated permissions. The attacks permit unauthorized topic access, forged GPS publication, door-control manipulation, workload termination, and physical robot crashes.
column8: Secs. 4.1–4.3, PDF pp. 4–6; Secs. 5.1–5.2, PDF pp. 7–8, Fig. 5; Secs. 6.2–6.3, PDF pp. 8–10, Figs. 6–7
column11: ROS2-ICAPP is preferred because the earliest root cause is the inadequate lifecycle protection and synchronization of permission policies between the owner, SROS2, and DDS layers. Unauthorized publishing and subscribing are consequences of this policy-protection failure. Both vulnerabilities are found through model-checking counterexamples and validated in simulation and on physical robots.

column2: On the (In)Security of Secure ROS2
column7: V3 shows that the default RTPS protection setting uses signing without encryption, allowing a malicious robot to recover node, topic, publisher, subscriber, and communication-topology information despite SROS2 being enabled. The authors exploit this configuration with a ROS 2 fingerprinting tool to infer robot positions, tasks, and control structures in simulated and physical workloads. V4 further shows that SROS2 permission files remain in plaintext and that official project templates often contain excessive information about other nodes and their topic permissions, enabling local policy and configuration disclosure.
column8: Sec. 2.4, PDF p. 3; Secs. 5.3–5.4, PDF p. 8; Secs. 6.2–6.3, PDF pp. 8–10, Fig. 8
column11: Full because information leakage is directly analyzed and exploited. V3 overlaps with previously reported DDS-related CVEs, but the paper independently demonstrates the effect within complete SROS2 robotic workloads. V4 is not merely a general least-privilege recommendation: the authors inspect official permission-file examples and demonstrate that their plaintext, over-inclusive contents disclose security information.

column2: ROSDiscover: Statically Detecting Run-Time Architecture Misconfigurations in Robotics Systems
column7: ROSDiscover detects inconsistent composition and configuration of ROS components, including mismatched topic names, incompatible publisher/subscriber message types, incorrect topic remappings, dangling communication endpoints, missing parameters and parameters configured with incompatible names, paths or types. The Autoware example in Figure 1 shows that renaming a publisher topic from line_class to line without updating subscribers disconnects the nodes and silently prevents message delivery. The evaluation corpus contains real configuration bugs from AutoRally, Autoware, MAVROS, Husky and TurtleBot.
column8: Sec. I–II, pp. 112–114; Fig. 1, p. 114; Sec. III, pp. 115–117; Sec. IV-C, pp. 119–120; Tables I and VI
column11: Primary and only defect code. The faults are reproduced from real historical commits and checked against corrected versions. They concern ROS component interfaces, connectors, parameters and launch-time composition.
